title: Only perpetual Christian consensus could count — Rome's traditions fail that test
source_text: XLIV. Denique, si qua traditio pro vera habenda sit, illa est quam commendat perpetuus & constans Christianorum consensus. Sed hoc minime convenit traditionibus Ecclesiae Romanae, quia non tantum sunt extra Scripturam, & in plerisque Scripturae adversantur, sed etiam earum plurimae sunt in Ecclesia antiqua inauditae, & ejus fidei & praxi contrariae. Cujus generis sunt indulgentiae, quales a Papa conceduntur, sanctorum canonizatio, celebratio cultus publici lingua non communiter a populo intellecta, prohibitio ne Scriptura sacra in vulgares linguas transferatur, & sine speciali permissione a plebe legatur: praecipue vero mos administrandi sacram Eucharistiam sub altero tantum symbolo, & plurium hujusmodi; item effingendi & cultu religioso prosequendi imagines Dei & sanctorum, quae facile est ostendere locum non habuisse in Ecclesia primitiva, & contrarium plane observatum fuisse. Unde manifeste patet illas esse commenta hominum, nec absque impietate posse cum Apostolorum & Prophetarum scriptis authoritate comparari.
pass_a_gloss: Finally, if any tradition is to be held as true, it is that which perpetual and constant consensus of Christians commends. But this by no means fits the traditions of the Roman Church, because they are not only outside Scripture, and in most things adverse to Scripture, but also many of them were unheard of in the ancient Church, and contrary to its faith and practice. Of this kind are indulgences such as are granted by the Pope, the canonization of saints, the celebration of public worship in a language not commonly understood by the people, the prohibition that sacred Scripture be translated into vulgar tongues and read by the people without special permission: and especially the custom of administering the sacred Eucharist under only one kind, and many things of this sort; likewise fashioning and religiously pursuing with worship images of God and of the saints, which it is easy to show had no place in the primitive Church, and that the contrary was plainly observed. From which it is manifestly plain that they are inventions of men, and cannot without impiety be compared in authority with the writings of the Apostles and Prophets.
pass_b_english: If any tradition deserves to be true, it is one marked by the perpetual, constant consensus of Christians.
Rome's traditions fail that test: they stand outside Scripture, often against it, and many were unknown in the ancient Church and contrary to its faith and practice.

Examples: papal indulgences; saint-canonization; public worship in a tongue the people do not share; bans on vernacular Scripture without special leave; communion in one kind; and religious image-making and image-worship — easy to show absent, even opposed, in the primitive Church.
So they are human inventions, and it is impious to set them equal in authority with the writings of Apostles and Prophets.
Pars II closes here; Pars III opens next.
